requirement at issue obligates certain employers to provide contraceptive 
coverage to their employees through their group health plans. * * * [T]he 
Government mandated such coverage by promulgating interim final rules 
(IFRs) shortly after the ACA’s passage. This requirement is known as the 
contraceptive mandate.
After six years of protracted litigation, the Departments of Health and 
Human Services, Labor, and the Treasury (Departments)—^which jointly 
administer the relevant ACA provision—exempted certain employers who 
have rehgious and conscientious objections from this agency-created 
mandate. The Third Circuit concluded that the Departments lacked 
statutory authority to promulgate these exemptions and affirmed the 
District Court’s nationwide preliminary injunction. This decision was 
erroneous. * * *
I
*** [In a series of rules promulgated under the ACA, the 
Departments set up the contraceptive mandate and made certain 
exemptions to it. Some of these rules took the form of Interim Final Rules 
(IFRs), that is, rules as to which “the Departments invoked the 
[Administrative Procedure Act’s] good cause exception, which permits an 
agency to dispense with notice and comment and promulgate an IFR that 
carries immediate legal force. § 553(b)(3)(B).” The mandate and 
exemptions were the object of extensive litigation that came before the 
Supreme Court in 2014 and again in 2016.]
* * * In 2017, the Departments * * * promulgat[ed] * * * the two 
[Interim Final Rules] that served as the impetus for this [case currently 
before the Supreme Court]. The first IFR significantly broadened the 
definition of an exempt religious employer to encompass an employer that 
“objects . . . based on its sincerely held religious beliefs,” “to its establishing, 
maintaining, providing, offering, or arranging [for] coverage or payments 
for some or all contraceptive services.” 82 Fed. Reg. 47812 (2017). Among 
other things, this definition included for-profit and publicly traded entities. 
* ie *
As with their previous regulations, the Departments * * * invoked 
§ 300gg-13(a)(4) [of the ACA] as authority to promulgate this “religious 
exemption,” stating that it “include[d] the ability to exempt entities from 
coverage requirements * * 
[82 Fed. Reg.] at 47794. Additionally, the
Departments announced for the first time that [the Religious Freedom 
Restoration Act of 1993 (RFRA)] compelled the creation of, or at least 
provided the discretion to create, the rehgious exemption. Id,, at 47800- 
47806.* * *
